preamble: In the Yugambeh-Bundjalung dialect chain of north-eastern New South Wales and south-eastern Queensland, the obstruents are realised more often as fricatives or affricates than as stops. Word-medially the palatal stop /ɟ/ (practical orthography j) and the apical stop /d/ collapse into a single sound, which is an interdental fricative in some dialects, an alveopalatal stop in others and a sibilant fricative in others (Sharpe 2005). Sharpe notes that dialect names such as Gidhabal were mostly named for the way some words were pronounced. This is allophonic lenition, and the obstruents are described as phonetically mostly voiceless, so the voiced value [ð] is approximate.

examples.note: Dialect-dependent merger of medial /ɟ/ with /d/ as an interdental fricative; other dialects have an alveopalatal stop or a sibilant fricative instead. No individual word forms could be verified online.

sources: Sharpe, M. (2005). Grammar and Texts of the Yugambeh-Bundjalung Dialect Chain in Eastern Australia. Languages of the World/Materials 370. Munich: Lincom. ISBN 3-89586-784-5. https://linguistlist.org/issues/16/2752/
